newsitem.title: FRANCE: French capital markets closing report.
newsitem.headline: French capital markets closing report.

text.p: Three-month interest rate futures settled sharply higher as worries over European monetary union eased amid hopes a compromise would be brokered allowing France to ratify the stability pact next week in Amsterdam.
June PIBOR gained five basis points to 96.42.
Ten-year bond futures also gained but were unable to break through resistance at 129.86/129.90 and profit-taking set in.
While market worries over ratification of the stability pact were receding, uncertainty about the new Socialist government's policies were capping gains, said one analyst.
He said it was unlikely the 10-year contract would be able to break through 130.00 between now and its expiry next Monday.
Short-covering propelled the 10-year future higher in early trade as renewed optimism about the stability pact caught investors on the hop, one trader said.

But there "are a lot of worries still dogging the market. It really doesn't have much direction. We've been in a trading range for some time and there is a lot of liquidity around but investors don't seem to want to invest," he said.
Some economists said optimism that France would sign up for the stability pact at the Amsterdam summit could be overdone.

Finance minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn said on Wednesday France wanted an early solution to the dispute over France's call for a greater focus on tackling unemployment before it ratifies the deal. But he said the question would be "how we can obtain the balance we are seeking" between budget discipline and growth and jobs.
"The market really wants to believe France will sign (in Amsterdam)," Credit Agricole Indosuez economist Arnaud Mares said. "I think they need to be more cautious."
Others, although surprised by the apparent compromise shaping up so soon after French leaders said they could not ratify the pact in Amsterdam, were more optimistic.
"It's very surprising. It's almost a U-turn. I think this may be reflective of a new government's teething problems -- that it is not consistent," said Sonja Gibbs of Nomura.
"I think the risks are more domestic both in France and Germany and relate to public opinion," she said.
One analyst said investor uncertainty over the government's new budget measures would stop PIBOR breaching resistance at 96.47.
The raft of U.S. figures, starting on May retail sales, could also have an impact on the market, another said.
The franc was relatively steady against the mark at 3.3828 but made good gains against the dollar, rising to 5.7970/80 per dollar compared with 5.8155/75 on Tuesday.
